blocks.text: It remains to add a few remarks on the various names of storks. The Hebrew חסידה hasida and the Greek πελαργὸς [pelargos] have already been fully explained. The Syriac ܚܘܪܒܐ hurba seems to have been formed by metathesis from ܚܘܒܪܐ hubra, which would mean the sociable bird. Of the Israelites it is said in Iud. XX, 11.: All the Israelites were gathered together, as one man, חברים, companions. See the same thing in Pliny about storks! When about to depart they gather in a fixed place, and they keep together in such a way that none of their kind is left behind, unless it is captive and enslaved. The Arabic لقلق [laqlaq] leklek and لغلغ [laghlagh] legleg were formed from the stork's cry, as the Arabs expressly teach. Damir: وصوته اللقلقه وكذلك كل صوت فيه حركه واضطراب [wa-ṣawtuhu al-laqlaqa wa-kadhālika kull ṣawt fīhi ḥaraka wa-iḍṭirāb] And laklaka is the cry of the stork, and every sound that is produced with vibration and agitation. Accordingly laklaka is also the name for the hiss of a serpent, produced with the tongue thrust out. Moreover, this cry of the stork does not come from deep in the throat, but is made by the two parts of the bill striking against each other, like a castanet or a rattle. Hence Publilius Syrus calls it crotalistria [castanet-player], and Ovid, in book 6 of the Metamorphoses, says

And Solinus wrote that the sound with which they rattle is of the mouth rather than of the voice. But he would have done better to say of the bill. Philostratus too, in his Letter to Epictetus: Καὶ τοὺς πελαργοὺς, ἐπειδὰν παριόντας ἡμᾶς κροτῶσιν [Kai tous pelargous, epeidan pariontas hēmas krotōsin], that is, The storks, when they rattle at us as we pass by. For the word there is κροτῶσιν [krotōsin], whence crotalistria. The Latin name CICONIA also goes back to the same thing. Isidore: Storks (CICONIAE) are so called, as if cicaniae, from the sound with which they rattle, which they make by shaking the bill. Nor is there any doubt that the Arabic العقعق [al-ʿaqʿaq] alkoko, which we explained above ^{i)}, alludes to this very thing.
